title: Bidirectional associations between executive function and social behavior across childhood: A registered report using a nationally representative sample.
description: Executive function (EF) refers to a set of cognitive skills involved in deliberate, goal-oriented behavior. Although research has established links between children’s EF and aspects of their social skills, it remains unclear how EF skills are related to specific social behaviors, such as prosociality and social aggression. Additionally, the co-development of EF and social behavior during childhood is less understood. Therefore, the current registered report aimed to examine bidirectional associations between two EF skills - working memory and cognitive flexibility - and children's prosocial behavior and social aggression using the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study - Kindergarten Class of 2010-11 (ECLS-K:2011; N = 18,174). Based on Sameroff’s Transactional Model of Human Development, we expected that EF and social behavior would be bidirectionally related from third-to-fifth grade (8 to 11 years old). We hypothesized that both working memory and cognitive flexibility would be positively associated with later prosocial behavior and negatively associated with later social aggression. Furthermore, we hypothesized that prosocial behavior would be positively associated with later EF skills and that social aggression would be negatively associated with later EF skills. Our results indicated that, at the between-person level, EF skills were positively associated with prosocial behavior and only working memory was negatively associated with social aggression. At the within-person level, we found no bidirectional associations between EF skills and social behaviors. However, we observed a small number of concurrent correlations between EF skills and social behaviors, along with a limited set of cross-lagged associations. Findings are discussed in the context of children’s social development.

title: Signatures proposed to index perceptual effects emerge in a purely cognitive task
description: A central question in many studies on perception and consciousness is whether the effects of a given manipulation are perceptual or cognitive. Typically, studies seek to find evidence that the raw sensory experience has been altered—that is, a manipulation produces perceptual rather than cognitive effects. Here, we test two specific proposals for behavioral signatures that could allow this type of inference. First, a long-standing proposition is that different parameters of the drift–diffusion model (DDM) map onto different effects, such that a drift-rate bias indicates a perceptual effect, whereas a starting point shift indicates a cognitive effect. Second, a newer proposal holds that, when plotted as a function of a sensory feature, changes in the peak of the distributions for confidence and reaction time (RT) imply that a given manipulation’s effects are perceptual. Here, we test both proposals. We designed a purely cognitive task where no effects can be perceptual and examined whether the proposed signatures of perceptual effects occur in this task. Participants viewed numbers generated by two distributions and indicated which distribution the numbers likely came from. In separate conditions we manipulated prior beliefs and rewards related to each distribution. We found that both manipulations elicited the same signatures previously proposed as indicative of purely perceptual effects. Our results demonstrate that individual DDM parameters and the peaks of confidence and RT distributions in isolation are insufficient to distinguish between perceptual and cognitive effects.

title: ManyBabies 6: A Multi-Lab Investigation of Neonatal and Early Imitation
description: Classic theory in developmental science holds that the imitation of facial gestures is a late developing capacity in human infancy. Meltzoff and Moore (1977) reported that 12- to 21-day-old infants imitate facial and manual gestures, theorizing that young infants can recognize cross-modal correspondences between observed and performed actions and suggesting that early imitation plays a role in social learning from other people. Subsequent studies yielded mixed findings and alternative interpretations have been proposed. Thus, whether young infants can imitate adult gestures remains a debated question. As part of the ManyBabies consortium, a large-scale collaborative network in developmental science, we tested whether very young infants (14–28 and 40–54 days old) demonstrate facial imitation using a protocol that was standardized for use across multiple independent laboratories. In a within-subjects design, infants saw mouth-opening and tongue-protrusion gestures in randomized order, presented by the same experimenter at the same distance and rate; responses were videorecorded for later behavioral scoring. title: Graded gender perceptions in personal names predict difficulty in reference resolution
description: We conducted two experiments to better understand how comprehenders use probabilistic knowledge of the associations between genders and personal names when inferring the gender of new referents during reading. Personal names are, surprisingly, under-investigated in studies on gender inference compared to role nouns (e.g., nurse) despite being strongly connected to gender. In a self-paced reading task involving variably gender biased names and gendered reflexives, we observe a gender mismatch effect proportional to the incongruence between a name’s perceived gender and that of the reflexive. In a novel variant of the Maze task involving forced ambiguity resolution between two gendered reflexives, we find decisions track the perceived gender of names and decisions take longer with more ambiguous names. We interpret the results to support a model in which comprehenders make graded, not categorical, inferences about gender during incremental comprehension, contrary to previous proposals.

title: Neurodiversity and learning in context: Development and validation of a self-report measure of engagement with learning activities (MELA)
description: While neurodivergent students’ learning engagement is recognised as important, there is not yet a suitable measure of engagement with learning activities to support research into inclusive teaching. This paper outlines the development and validation of a new self-report instrument (MELA: Measure of Engagement with Learning Activities) intended for exploring neurodivergent students’ engagement. In Phase 1, existing measures were adapted and presented to autistic undergraduates (n = 33) and experts (n = 5). The measure was then refined following interviews with autistic students (n = 7) and presented in Phase 2 to autistic (n = 53) and non-autistic (n = 121) undergraduates to test for convergent validity through comparison against exiting measures. In Phase 3, the measure’s reliability and performance were examined. MELA demonstrated strong validity and therefore provides a robust research instrument for exploring students’ learning engagement, making it valuable for inclusion research supporting improvements to teaching in higher education.

title: Choose your own PAS? Quantitative and Qualitative Validity Evidence for the Perceptual Awareness Scale
description: The most preferred visibility measure in unconscious processing studies is the Perceptual Awareness Scale (PAS). Since it was originally proposed as a methodological approach, no PAS labels, instructions or display are currently official. Authors tend to adapt this scale to their experimental tasks often without specifying their PAS properties or without providing adequate justification for the modifications. In this work, we tested how “choosing your own PAS” affects response-process validity both quantitatively and qualitatively, in the same  unconscious working memory (WM) task as in Franco-Martínez et al. (in press) replication. In a preregistered 2×2×2 between-subjects design (N = 176), we manipulated: PAS Version (Original vs New labels, updated based on pilot participants’ reports), Examples (With brief demonstrations of PAS = 4 and PAS = 1 trials vs Without them), and Display (Scale&Text shown onscreen trial-by-trial vs ScaleOnly). In a post-experiment PAS questionnaire participants were asked to qualitatively report how they recalled and interpreted the scale. The unconscious WM effect and its reliability were robust under the Version and Examples manipulations, but presenting the New Version and/or With Examples increased the proportion of valid trials, enhancing statistical power. Although the unconscious WM effect increased in the ScaleOnly Display, the qualitative evidence suggests participants in this condition tend to forget the PAS labels and ultimately use them differently from intended. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for the use of PAS and a post-experiment PAS questionnaire to evaluate its validity.

title: Adaptive search promotes asymmetrical learning
description: Recent theoretical work has argued that learning trajectories are shaped by adaptive search and satisficing. The central idea of this work is that the value of an information source (i.e., its utility or valence) modulates engagement, sampling density, and encoding fidelity, providing a behavioural pathway to variation in learning outcomes. The current manuscript reports the first explicit empirical test of this idea in adults using a modified version of a multi-step decision-making paradigm known as 'Mouselab'. Across two experiments and six sub-tasks, N=101 participants searched a decision tree at a cost until settling on and executing a high-value policy. While Experiment 1 involved a non-symbolic decision space, Experiment 2 incorporated symbolic cues that allowed us to determine the extent to which associative learning is sensitive to underlying value structure. We found that value-sensitive adaptive search promoted rank-dependent learning asymmetries at test – estimates for the value of the best symbol were near veridical, while those for low-value symbols were at chance. In addition, we found that (i) informative symbolic cues shifted search from balanced exploration (breadth ≈ depth) towards depth-first exploitation; (ii) cue-guided search developed rapidly, with high-value symbol exploitation emerging within a handful of trials; (iii) search evidenced a win-stay tendency and was sensitive to cue valence, with individuals quickly pruning negatively valued branches; (iv) raising cost constrained search volume but preserved its depth-first, cue-sensitive character; and (v) observed individual differences in search behaviour were not predicted by common measures of cognitive function. These results provide new insight into how adaptive search and satisficing shape learning, supporting an emerging theory of the behavioural origins of individual differences in human development.

title: Do LLMs Reliably Identify Correct Information Units in Aphasic Discourse?
description:
Purpose: Correct Information Units (CIUs) are central to discourse assessment in aphasia because they quantify
communicative informativeness rather than linguistic form alone. However, CIU scoring is time intensive and
requires trained raters. This study examined whether instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) can reliably
perform token-level CIU classification from aphasic discourse transcripts.
Method: Sixteen picture-description transcripts elicited with the Cat Rescue stimulus were annotated for CIU
status according to Nicholas and Brookshire (1993). The sample spanned four severity strata: control, mild,
moderate, and severe aphasia. Four publicly available instruction-tuned LLMs were benchmarked under zero-shot
and two few-shot prompting conditions across five stratified random seeds. Performance was evaluated against
consensus human labels using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and Cohen’s kappa.
Results: Zero-shot prompting was insufficient across models. In contrast, few-shot prompting yielded substantial
gains and produced competitive performance for three viable models. Mean few-shot F1 scores ranged from 0.776
to 0.817 across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B, with no significant differences between fixed global
and per-chunk local example selection. Phi-3-mini was unstable and did not yield reliable performance. Viable
models showed high recall but lower precision, suggesting systematic over-classification of tokens as CIUs.
Performance also varied by discourse severity, with the weakest results in more severe aphasia.
Conclusion: Few-shot LLM prompting can support automated CIU identification without gradient-based task
training, but agreement with human annotation remains insufficient for fully autonomous use. These findings
support LLM-based CIU scoring as a promising human-in-the-loop component of clinician-forward discourse
assessment systems.

title: Community Notes as debunking intervention: Correction design and topic context determine effectiveness
description: Crowdsourced on-platform corrections, such as Community Notes, have gained popularity as a scalable response to misinformation. Yet it remains unclear whether they function as effective debunking interventions. This study investigates whether corrections presented in the forms of Community Notes reduce continued influence of misinformation and whether their effectiveness varies across neutral and socially divisive content. In an online experiment, 542 adults from a quota-based German sample viewed simulated social media posts containing misinformation. The misinformation was shown again with a Community Note in one of three forms: no correction, a simple retraction, or a retraction with an alternative explanation. For neutral content, both corrective notes reduced reliance on misinformation, with explanatory notes performing best. For socially divisive content, Community Notes reduced continued influence only when providing an alternative explanation. These findings suggest that Community Notes can serve as an effective debunking intervention, but only under specific design and context conditions.

title: The mental health emergency of heatwaves: Implications for Australian policy, clinical practice and social support
description: As climate change drives more frequent and severe heatwaves, its impacts on population mental health are becoming increasingly evident. Extreme heat is associated with increased psychological distress, aggression, suicide, and mental health-related service use. The risks are further heightened among people with pre-existing mental illness, due to physiological, social, and medication-related factors. Drawing on a rapid survey of Australian state and national heat-health policies, this perspective highlights the gap in integrating mental health into heatwave responses and outlines actionable recommendations to embed mental health within preparedness and response policies, clinical care, and community-based strategies in a warming climate.

title: Mental Well-Being and Stress in Farming Communities in the UK and Canada: The Roles of Personal Vulnerability and Event Load
description:
Objective: Farmers, their families, and employees face daily stressors that adversely affect their mental well-being. To improve understanding of stress and mental well-being in farming populations, this study examines this relationship in the United Kingdom (UK) and Canada. 
Method: Using an online cross-sectional survey, 569 adults from farming communities (37% male, 63% female; Mage = 47.57, SD = 12.55) completed measures of stress event load (EL), personal vulnerability to stress (PV), and subjective mental well-being. Data were analysed using analysis of variance and hierarchical multiple regression, with simple-slopes analysis. 
Results: Farming community members who reported higher PV reported significantly lower well-being, regardless of whether EL was low or high. In regression, when considered together, PV eliminated the predictive power of EL, highlighting the importance of PV. Although a significant interaction was observed, after Bonferroni correction, significance remained only for those with high PV, where well-being among farming community members was substantially lower than at low or average PV, across all levels of EL. While UK participants reported significantly lower mental well-being than Canadian participants, mental well-being was low in both countries at levels that necessitate support. 
Conclusion: While studies have traditionally focused on farming-specific causes of stress, personal vulnerability was a stronger determinant of mental well-being than stress event load across the two countries. Interventions targeting the psychological mechanisms that underpin stress appraisal will therefore help protect mental well-being in farming communities. Future research must utilise longitudinal measurements to explore the psychological resources of farming community members worldwide.

title: People Overestimate Support for “Cancellation”
description: Social exclusion has long served as a mechanism of norm enforcement. However, in contemporary discourse, there is a common narrative about “cancel culture” that implies an overextension of social exclusion – often driven by social media. Given the ambiguity surrounding what cancellation entails and how often it occurs, people may struggle to accurately judge their own likelihood of being cancelled for expressing controversial views. Across two preregistered studies (NS1 = 753, NS2 = 753), we examined judgments of cancellation using naturalistic statements that participants (N  = 49) in a pretest believed could get them “cancelled.” We found that people think they are more likely to get cancelled for making statements than is warranted, both when compared with other people’s judgment of the same statement and with others’ expressed willingness to impose such sanctions. Their estimates are also only weakly related to how others judged the same statement. Although participants generally judged cancellation as similarly likely whether they imagined themselves or another person making a statement, this self-other asymmetry emerged once cancellation was framed explicitly as taking place on social media: participants then perceived a greater likelihood of cancellation when simply imagining themselves, rather than another person, making the same statement. Together, these findings suggest that people systematically overestimate the risk of being cancelled and raise the possibility that concerns about cancellation are fueled by inaccurate beliefs about others’ willingness to impose social sanctions.

title: The recoverability, reliability and generalisability of reward processing parameters and relation to mental health symptoms
description: Theory-driven computational psychiatry attempts to use cognitive models of computation to understand how mental health problems might relate to (or be caused by) changes in cognitive processes such as learning and decision-making. However, the potential applications and relevance of this approach are contingent on several (often implicit) assumptions, including that computational parameters 1) are recoverable, 2) are reliable over time, 3) reflect conceptually similar processes across different tasks, and 4) relate to symptoms. To illustrate and test these assumptions for a selection of commonly used tasks, we recruited a large online sample of participants (n=548), who completed seven mental health questionnaires and five tasks. A subset of n=115 was re-invited to complete the five tasks 14 days later. For each task, five models (including a null model, or model of no interest) were fit and the winning model was selected through Bayesian model comparison. The parameters from the winning models showed good recovery (mean r=0.853, sd=0.135), and good to excellent levels of test-retest reliability (mean ICC=0.635, sd=0.30). Parameters that were theoretically or mathematically similar to each other were, however, generally not related, with relationships only found within the class of ‘inverse temperature’-like parameters (significant r values ranged from 0.11 to 0.23): indicating that in general, parameters do not generalise across task contexts. Finally, only parameters from two of the five tasks (four-armed bandit and cognitive effort) related to symptoms, and these relationships were weak (maximum absolute r values ~0.10). To conclude, it seems that at least some of the implicit assumptions when advocating for the use of computational models in psychiatry are not met for these popular tasks and computational models. title: Dyadic Affect Recovery Model: Parent-Adolescent Affect Inertia and Synchrony as  Risk Factors for Depressive Symptoms
description:
Ineffective regulation of negative affect is a risk factor for adolescent depression. Affect 
regulation is reflected in affect dynamics over time. This study extends this perspective by 
introducing a dyadic approach, as adolescents and their parents jointly navigate affect. Thus,
both individual and dyadic affect dynamics may influence adolescent mental health. In 2024-
25, 540 Dutch parent-adolescent dyads (adolescents: Mean age = 14.17 years, 54% girls; 
parent: Mean age = 46.62, 83% mothers) reported current negative affect 5-6 times daily for 
three weeks and daily negative affect across 100 days. Hourly and daily negative affect 
inertia (i.e., affect autocorrelation) and dyadic affect synchrony (i.e., dyadic affect 
correlation) were estimated from 63,297 hourly and 71,060 daily reports. Analyses of hourly 
and daily affect dynamics showed that adolescent depression was associated with greater 
affect inertia from both adolescents and parents at both timescales. Hourly affect synchrony 
was associated with fewer depressive symptoms, whereas daily synchrony was associated 
with more depressive symptoms. Controlling for mean affect, greater adolescent depressive 
symptoms remained associated with higher hourly adolescent affect inertia and higher daily 
affect synchrony. Two major conclusions emerged. First, negative affect dynamics reflected
mental health beyond mean levels of affect. Second, individual and dyadic affect dynamics 
were both relevant for mental health, but operated on different timescales. Future research 
might further examine the role of the family system in adolescent depression

title: PARADOx: A Randomized Controlled Trial Examining Short- and Long-Term, Family-Specific, and Side Effects of a Digital Parenting Intervention
description: Few digital parenting interventions for preventing adolescent mental health problems exist and little is known about their effectiveness. This preregistered Randomized Controlled Trial examined short-term (1 month post-intervention) and longer-term (6 months) effects, side-effects, and family-specific effects of a novel digital parenting intervention. Dutch adolescents (N = 547, 53% female, Mage = 14.1) and one of their parents (N = 541; 81% mothers, Mage = 46.7) were assigned to a control or intervention group. The intervention group received a parenting feedback report and 18 parenting tips across six weeks, in the second half of a 100-day diary study. No explicit intervention effects were identified, but no harmful side-effects were identified either. At 6-month follow-up, parent- and adolescent-reported overprotection decreased and longer-term adolescent well-being improved. Furthermore, improvements in overprotection and adolescent well-being were correlated and changes in overparenting were generally stronger when parents were exposed to more tips, tentatively suggesting a benefit of 100 days of journaling. The trial was retrospectively registered (CCMO; registration NL-009451) on 19-02-2025.

title: Manipulating Causal Priors Affects the Outcome-Density Bias
description: Non-contingent learning data can lead to the (seemingly) illusory perception of causality if the potential cause and effect often co-occur – an effect known as “outcome-density bias.” Bayesian models of causal induction explain this effect as the result of a rational learning process in which the data do not fully override non-zero causal priors. Convincing evidence for this rational explanation requires the demonstration of an experimentally manipulated effect of causal priors, which has been lacking. We successfully manipulated participants’ (𝑁 = 300) causal priors through visually conveyed causal mechanism information. This manipulation influenced the outcome-density effect in the predicted way: in a condition inducing low causal priors, the effect disappeared. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of visual mechanism information in manipulating priors and strengthen the Bayesian view of causal induction.

title: An Experimental Paradigm for Evaluating Shared Agency in Humans and LLMs
description: Coordination is central to social life, yet LLMs are poor coordinators. We introduce the Hangman game as a novel experimental paradigm to study why. Our focus is on shared agency, a precondition for coordination, defined as the ability to form shared goals, intentions, and plans. Success in Hangman requires agents to coordinate on word choices across rounds. Human teams reliably develop shared strategies, coordinating on mutually predictable word patterns. LLMs fail to do so. Across Human-Human, Human-LLM, and LLM-LLM teams, humans outperform all tested state-of-the-art LLMs, and humans paired with LLMs perform worse than when paired with other humans. As LLMs are increasingly deployed as collaborative agents, coordination failures undermine their usefulness. Hangman offers a flexible, controlled method for measuring and tracking coordination skills as models develop.

title: An Evolution of the UCLA Isolation Scales: Distinguishing Feelings of Loneliness from Social Disconnection in UK and US Online Adult Samples
description: Loneliness measurement has faced serious challenges in recent years, and recent reviews have cited indeterminate factor structures and poor construct validity as the principal causes. The field's most widely used instrument, the Revised UCLA Loneliness Scale (R-UCLA), has come under particular scrutiny. We address these challenges, firstly by clarifying the structure of the UCLA, and then by redeveloping it through a scale purification process (N = 21,589) in which we prune cross-loading items to create the UCLA-V (“UCLA-Five”). We confirm that the new scale behaves consistently across gender, geographic regions and age groups, and that it is functionally and structurally equivalent to its predecessor, but with a clear structure and improved model fit. We also derive the UCLA-V-short, the first true three-item representation of the UCLA (rparent = .92). We validate these scales in a multi-rater follow-up study (N = 910), finding that the UCLA is an isolation scale with three dimensions, one of which is loneliness.

title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain
description: The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to perceptual absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding absence as a concept – in the form of the number zero – has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography (MEG) to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct to those evoked by perceptual absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

title: Artificial intelligence as work design: A scoping review of motivational and demotivational mechanisms in professional work contexts
description:
Work design has long been recognized as a central determinant of intrinsic motivation, well-being, and performance. As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly enters professional work, it should not be understood merely as a technical tool, but as a force that directly reshapes working conditions by altering how tasks are structured, decisions are made, feedback is delivered, and workers interact with their work and with one another. This makes work design and motivational theories especially important for the design and implementation of AI systems. To clarify this fragmented field within human-AI interaction research, including closely related work on human-AI collaboration and human-AI teaming, we conducted a scoping review of AI in professional, knowledge-intensive work contexts, focusing on how different AI configurations relate to motivation and demotivation. Following PRISMA-ScR, we reviewed 31 empirical and non-empirical sources published between 2009 and 2025.
Only three sources proposed explicit motivational AI design frameworks, suggesting that motivation is still more often treated as an outcome of AI use than as a direct design objective. Across the corpus, AI was described as motivationally supportive when it preserved meaningful human influence, provided developmental feedback, or reduced routine burden without hollowing out meaningful work. Demotivational risks were described when AI expanded surveillance, narrowed self-organization, prescribed work too tightly, or translated social relations into comparison and performance signals. These risks were especially prominent in conceptual discussions of managerial or algorithmic-management configurations, whereas empirical evidence was more concentrated in assistive AI settings.

title: The Medusa Effect Revisited
description: The Medusa effect refers to the cognitive phenomenon in which individuals depicted directly in a photograph (Level 1; L1) are judged as possessing more mind than individuals depicted within a photograph embedded inside another photograph (Level 2; L2). Although the Medusa effect has been replicated in several studies, a number of issues still remain to be addressed. One concerns the measurement scale used for mind perception, and another concerns the size of the face and body of the person depicted in the stimulus images. The present study addressed these unresolved issues across three experiments. Experiment 1 examined whether the Medusa effect could be replicated using the 18 concrete mental capacity items derived from Gray et al. (2007). Results showed that L1 targets were judged as possessing greater mental capacities than L2 targets across several capacities, particularly Agency-related capacities. Experiment 2 tested whether this effect would persist when L1 and L2 targets were presented at equal displayed sizes. Under size-controlled conditions, the Medusa effect was not observed. Experiment 3 independently manipulated target size and hierarchical frame cues. Presentation size showed significant main effects across multiple mental capacity judgments, whereas frame presence showed no reliable main effects. Together, these findings suggest that stimulus size contributes substantially to previously reported Medusa effect when mind perception is assessed using concrete mental capacity items.

title: How Schemas Shape Memory for Everyday Activities: The Roles of Surprise and Prediction  Uncertainty
description:
Schemas provide structured knowledge that guides comprehension and memory of 
everyday experience. Schema violations have powerful effects on memory, but sometimes 
in apparently opposing directions—schema consistency can apparently boost or impair 
memory. We used narrative texts describing everyday activities to try to resolve the 
apparently conflicting effects. We investigated three fundamental issues: how schema 
consistency and violation affect memory formation, what dimensions of schema violation 
contribute to subjective surprise, and how prediction uncertainty influences memory 
encoding. In Study 1, gist but not detail memory was monotonically better for more 
surprising events. This is consistent with the proposal that schema violations trigger 
additional processing, but not with the proposal that schema-consistent information 
garners any advantageous processing. Schema-consistent information was not forgotten 
more slowly over 24 hours. Study 2 investigated factors leading to schema-driven surprise. 
Surprise was driven primarily by an event's appropriateness (contextual fit) rather than its 
relevance to activity goals. Critically, inappropriate events elicited stronger surprise when 
they occurred during goal-relevant actions, consistent with predictive processing theories, 
suggesting that humans develop more precise predictions about functionally important 
aspects of activities. In Study 3, gist memory was better for high-uncertainty information, 
supporting proposals that additional attention is allocated to moments of uncertainty. 
Together, these findings suggest that gist memory is enhanced when events are surprising 
or uncertain, and that surprise arises from contextual inappropriateness modulated by goal 
relevance.

title: Non-linear Sensitivity to Binaural Interaural Correlation Changes: The Impact of Correlation Change and Interaural Delay
description:
Human listeners’ ability to detect a binaural interaural correlation (BIAC) change is crucial for auditory scene analysis. The present study investigated whether human listeners can detect a binaurally correlation-changed arbitrary-noise fragment [a ‘break’ in correlation, break in interaural correlation (BIAC)] embedded in binaurally steady-noise markers, and further examined how this detection sensitivity is modulated by different levels of correlation change. The longest interaural delay was used to index the BIAC detection sensitivity.
In Experiment 1, twenty-three normal-hearing participants were tested for the longest interaural delay remained to detect a binaurally correlation-changed arbitrary-noise fragment embedded in identical arbitrary-noise (BIAC fragment correlations: 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8). In Experiment 2, another twenty normal-hearing participants were tested for the longest interaural delay remained to detect a binaurally uncorrelated arbitrary-noise fragment in steady-noise (the background steady-noise correlations: 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1). 
As the BIAC correlation level increased, the longest interaural delay remained to detect the BIAC in identical noises decreased significantly (Exp 1); conversely, as the background steady-noise correlation level increased, the longest interaural delay remained to detect the uncorrelated BIAC increased significantly (Exp 2). Results showed that detection sensitivity is non-linearly modulated in both cases. Specifically, thresholds followed exponential decay (Exp 1) and growth (Exp 2) models, revealing a "mutation" in sensitivity as correlation contrast decreased. These findings suggest that people could detect a BIAC in steady-noise markers with binaural delay whether the correlation of BIAC fragment or background decrease, and this sensitivity was nonlinearly modulated by the magnitude of correlation change.

title: Disrupted Geometric Constraints on Connectome Wiring in Children and Adolescents with ADHD
description: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is thought to result from aberrant neurodevelopmental wiring of connectome architecture, yet the precise mechanisms underpinning this miswiring remain unclear. Here, we used a generative mathematical model to understand how physical and geometric constraints on brain network development might be altered in the disorder. Leveraging multisite diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) datasets comprising 713 ADHD children and 304 neurotypical controls (aged 6-18 years), we fitted the recently developed geometric eigenmode model (GEM) to individual data describing connectivity between each pair of cortical regions, as quantified using probabilistic tractography. Replicating past work, the GEM was able to recover both topological and topographical properties of the empirical connectomes, but reconstruction accuracy was lower in ADHD children, suggesting a relative untethering of connectome architecture from geometric constraints. This untethering was particularly salient for long-range connections, which were disproportionately affected in the ADHD cohort. Regional variations in the degree to which connectivity was untethered from geometry were correlated with spatial maps of cortical developmental expansion, myelination, and transcriptomic organization, consistent with a neurodevelopmental basis for geometric untethering that is spatially patterned along the cortical hierarchy. Together, these findings suggest that aberrant neurodevelopment in ADHD may untether connectome development from typical geometric and physical constraints, resulting in subtle disruptions of long-range inter-regional connectivity.

title: Can conversational AI influence confidence in pre-existing political beliefs?
description: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) may influence political polarization by shaping the strength with which political attitudes are held. Generative AI systems are increasingly capable of conducting adaptive, human-like conversations, raising questions about their ability to strengthen or weaken belief certainty. We report results from a preregistered, two-wave randomized experiment (N = 1,968) testing whether GPT-4 can strengthen or weaken individuals' attitudes on salient, evolving political issues. Participants engaged in personalized, multi-turn conversations in which the AI was instructed to either strengthen or weaken their stated views, or to engage in non-political discussion. Across issues including housing, immigration, and economic policy, AI-mediated conversations consistently reduced attitude strength. Specifically, belief confidence, while showing no evidence of strengthening. These effects persisted for up to 21 days. Our findings indicate that generative AI can durably influence political attitudes, primarily by weakening rather than strengthening belief certainty. By examining both pro and counter-attitudinal persuasion among individuals with existing views in dynamic political contexts, this study provides a demanding test of AI’s persuasive capacity and clarifies its implications for political polarization and democratic discourse.

title: Innovations in Practice: A Pilot Randomised Trial on Smartphone and Social Media Abstinence: Effects on Sleep Quality and Psychological Well-being in Adolescents
description: There is growing concern that smartphones and social media (S/SM) disrupt adolescent sleep, wellbeing and cognition, yet causal evidence from robust interventions is limited. To assess the acceptability of a total 21-day S/SM detox we conducted a preregistered (https://osf.io/79zd2) pilot randomised control trial with eighty-two adolescents aged 13-18 years from UK schools. Participants were randomly assigned to a total S/SM detox (N=26), total S/SM detox with access to a basic “brick” phone (N=26) or a business-as-usual control (N=30). Pre-and post-intervention measures of sleep, wellbeing, and cognition were collected using surveys, wearables, and cognitive tasks.  Retention was high, with 13% attrition across groups. At 21-days, one or both detox groups showed tentative improvements in sleep duration, daytime sleepiness, depressive symptoms, perceived stress, and working memory relative to the controls, however these changes were not maintained at a two-month follow-up. Open-ended post-detox reflections reflected a range of both positive and negative experiences, with reported challenges including boredom, functional reliance on smartphones, and fear of missing out.  Nevertheless, 83% endorsed the need for government action. Digital detoxes appear feasible for generating causal evidence; however, they can also pose functional challenges to young people. Fully powered trials should address these challenges, potentially via more targeted intervention approaches (e.g. switching off the internet on smartphones, particularly at bed-time).

title: Motivation Science in Digital and AI-Supported Learning Environments
description: In this conceptual paper, we argue that motivation science provides a valuable yet underutilized framework for understanding and designing digital and AI-supported learning environments. To illustrate this, we first review studies included in a recent meta-analysis on generative AI and motivation to examine the extent to which motivation science informs current research. We show that the vast majority of studies do not use motivational theories to explain how such systems may support student motivation. Next, drawing primarily on achievement goal theory and the TARGET (task, autonomy, grouping, recognition, time) framework, we outline key motivational principles for structuring learning environments and discuss how these principles may be enacted in digital and AI-supported contexts. We also examine risks and tensions associated with these environments, acknowledging that digital and AI systems may create novel motivational challenges not fully addressed by existing motivational theories developed in more traditional educational settings. Overall, the paper aims to stimulate further research on rethinking digital and AI-supported learning environments through the lens of motivation science while also reconsidering motivation science in light of these emerging environments.

title: Can callous-unemotional (CU) traits be acquired? Tests in a longitudinal sample spanning late childhood through adolescence
description: Background. Callous-unemotional (CU) traits (i.e., “Limited Prosocial Emotions”) characterize a particularly severe group of antisocial youth. “Secondary” CU traits, as opposed to “primary,” are distinguished by co-occurring anxiety and are theorized to reflect an acquired phenotype that develops through an interaction between heightened emotional sensitivity and prolonged adversity exposure. The aim of this study was to test this pathway in a large, diverse sample spanning late childhood (age 9-10) to middle adolescence. Methods. Data were drawn from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, with youth (N = 11, 880; Mage = 10; 48% female) assessed annually over five timepoints. Retrospective and prospective analyses examined the effects of emotional sensitivity and different forms of adversity on the development of CU traits. Results. Retrospective analyses showed no main or interactive effects of emotional sensitivity and adversity during late childhood in predicting secondary CU traits by adolescence. Instead, a significant interaction (B = .21, SE = .06, p < .001, RRR = 1.24) was found such that higher overall adversity and emotional sensitivity together increased risk for primary, not secondary, CU traits. Prospective analyses among emotionally sensitive (≥90th percentile) youth with no CU traits (n = 365, age ~10) similarly showed no forms of cumulative adversity predicted increases in or the onset of “elevated” CU traits after four years. Conclusions. Findings did not support a distinct adversity-linked pathway to secondary CU traits via emotional sensitivity. Instead, results were consistent with alternative models in which secondary CU traits reflect a comorbid profile marked by broader clinical severity or overlapping liabilities (e.g., negative affectivity, internalizing risk).

title: Semantigories: A large-scale investigation of form-meaning interactions and category-level differences in semantic memory search
description: Humans routinely search for information within their mental lexicon, and this process involves navigating across clusters of related items within a complex lexical landscape. However, concepts can be related in several ways, and prior work has examined semantic memory search primarily within taxonomic categories (e.g., Animals) and underemphasized interactions between lexical sources that guide search and retrieval. The present work examined memory search via the verbal fluency task across different semantic categories as an explore-exploit trade-off mediated by semantic, phonological, and frequency-based information within the lexicon. This account was tested on a large-scale compilation of semantic fluency data (N=1245) across six diverse categorical domains (Animals, Occupations, Things at the Beach, Things in a Classroom, Things to Rescue from a Burning Home and Excuses for Being Late), being made openly available for future research via https://semantigories.research.bowdoin.edu/. Search behavior was consistent with a strategic foraging account within the taxonomic category Animals, whereas search in categories with less rigid organization was relatively impaired, highly idiosyncratic, and relied more on short-range transitions indicating a strong tendency to select the most similar and accessible items. Fluency performance was enhanced for individuals who adequately leveraged form-meaning mappings within structured and functional categories, suggesting that memory search involves both automatic and strategic components. The present results thus highlight the flexibility of both semantic representations and search processes in human cognition.

title: Look at Me Being Good – Connecting Moral Grandstanding with Affective Polarization and Civic Engagement
description: In polarized societies where public moral discourse is often performed in front of broad audiences, understanding the psychological dynamics of moral grandstanding has become crucial for explaining both social division and civic engagement. Moral grandstanding, defined as the use of moral and political discourse to seek social status, has been linked to affective polarization, yet less is known about how this moralized self-presentation relates to civic engagement and helping behavior. Across four studies (N total = 1720), we examine how moral grandstanding is associated with affective polarization and different forms of helping in the context of refugee support and intergroup relations. Study 1 (N = 503) replicates previous findings showing that moral grandstanding positively predicts affective polarization, even when controlling for intellectual humility. Study 2 (N = 774) demonstrates that dichotomous thinking is statistically implicated in the association between moral grandstanding and affective polarization, including in a more right-leaning sample. Study 3 (N = 212) shows that moral grandstanding is positively related to both dependency-oriented and autonomy-oriented helping intentions, as well as to public and private forms of intergroup civic engagement; these associations are partially mediated by affective polarization. Study 4 focuses on a sample of self-identified activists (N = 231) and reveals that moral grandstanding is not only positively associated with reported intentions to help – both in dependency- and autonomy-oriented ways – but also with self-reported past helping behavior.

title: The Development of Superstitions in Uncontrollable Environment
description: Superstitions are false beliefs about causality and illusory control over outcomes. Although previous research has explored factors that influence superstitious beliefs, the cognitive processes underlying their formation remain unclear. We designed a task environment allowing free exploration of a vast number of actions with uncontrollable outcomes to understand the development of superstitions over experience. Participants (N=281) played a game where they attempted to produce rewarding keypress sequences across 100 trials with randomly assigned reward contingencies, reporting perceived reward probability and controllability. We found that perceived controllability increased non-linearly with reward rates, plateauing after 50%. Reward predictions and controllability showed a bidirectional feedback loop, reinforcing each other. Personality traits such as superstition proneness, locus of control, and schizotypy also influenced perceived controllability. Our results delineate how superstitious beliefs emerge from an interplay between environmental reward statistics, exploratory tendencies, and psychological traits, involving distorted perceptions of causality.

title: The Affective Nature of Affective Polarization: Evidence from Physiological and Self-Reported Responses to U.S. Politicians
description: What is the nature of affective partisan polarization? We answer this question in a preregistered laboratory study conducted in the United States measuring partisans' affective reactions tostatic images of U.S. politicians with self-reports and physiological indicators of valence and arousal. Consistent with prior research, participants reported substantially more negative evaluations of out-party than in-party politicians. However, we do not observe reliable physiological differentiation between in-party and out-party elites under these conditions. This disconnect between self-reported negative affect and concurrent physiological responses suggests that, in the context of minimal elite exposure, affective polarization can be expressed without detectable visceral activation. These findings are consistent with constructivist and attitude-retrieval accounts and constrain strong versions of the hot cognition thesis, though they do not logically exclude all possible roles for visceral affect under different conditions.

title: Chronotype and Daily Social Connectedness: Insights from a 30-Day Diary Study
description: Chronotype refers to individual preferences regarding the timing of activity and rest within the circadian cycle. Previous research has demonstrated its associations with various aspects of social functioning. The present study examines how chronotype is related to daily feelings of social connectedness. A total of N = 224 participants (M = 47.66, SD = 17.57) were recruited. At baseline, participants completed the Morningness-Eveningness-Stability-Scale improved (MESSi), followed by 30 consecutive days of social connectedness assessments using a short version of the UBC State Social Connection Scale (UBC-SSCS). Analyses revealed that higher morning affect was associated both with higher overall levels and lower day-to-day variability in social connectedness. In contrast, higher distinctness was related to lower average levels of social connectedness and greater fluctuations across days. No significant associations were found between eveningness and social connectedness. These findings highlight the importance of morning affect, and crucially, circadian stability in contributing to individuals’ perceived connection with others.

title: Exploring the Influence of Music’s Semantic Associations on Autobiographical Memories
description:
While the effect of music on autobiographical memories has been examined in the past, it has not 
yet been studied how semantic associations with music cues influence the content and 
phenomenology of autobiographical memories. In a repeated-measures design experiment with 
53 participants, we tested how 14 musical cues depicting semantic associations, in either a more 
concrete (e.g., “birds”) or abstract (e.g., “French café ambience”) manner, influenced the recall 
of autobiographical memories and the phenomenological characteristics of these. Some music 
excerpts evoked a high proportion of memories containing our expected semantic association 
(e.g. “Loss” and “Latin-American ambience”). Others were less successful in evoking the 
expected semantic association, but nevertheless evoked memories with a high degree of shared 
content (e.g., “Calmness”). There were no statistically significant differences found in the 
phenomenological characteristics of the memories evoked by more concrete versus abstract 
music cues. These results indicate that music can convey shared semantic meaning across 
listeners that shapes the content of associated memories, although this capacity varies 
substantially across different musical cues. Findings from this study have implications for how 
music may be used as a memory cue in comparison to other cue types in both clinical and 
everyday settings.

title: Perinatal Engagement With a Purpose-Built AI for Mental Health (Ash): Emotional Expression, Help-Seeking, and Estimated Depression Trajectories Across Pregnancy and Postpartum
description:
Objective: Perinatal mood disorders are common and consequential yet underdiagnosed and undertreated. Conversational AI mental health tools may help close this gap, but real-world evidence on how perinatal individuals engage with them remains limited. We aimed to characterize naturalistic engagement with a purpose-built mental health AI tool (Ash) across the perinatal period, using a theory-informed emotion taxonomy and predicted depression-severity trajectories.

Methods & Analysis: We conducted a retrospective analysis of conversation logs (May 2025-January 2026). An LLM classifier followed by clinical psychologist review of every classifier-positive case yielded 419 confirmed perinatal users (4,087 sessions). Sessions were coded by an LLM judge against a 26-label, six-domain Perinatal Emotion Expression Taxonomy anchored in established perinatal theory. A separate model produced continuous PHQ-9 estimates over two-week windows. A date-matched cohort of 46,134 non-perinatal users served as comparison, and all high- and crisis-risk sessions received blinded clinician review of AI escalation.

Results: Perinatal users differed from the general cohort by content (parenting d = +1.34, family d = +0.72) rather than overall distress. Sessions were emotionally multidimensional (mean 5.38 labels; 77.8% endorsed ≥3 concurrent) with relational and attachment content dominant (75.9%). Distress followed a non-monotonic course with two troughs (second trimester; 6 weeks-3 months postpartum). Across the postpartum year, positive affect declined and identity/role strain and emotional exhaustion rose monotonically. Among users entering at moderate severity or above, model-estimated PHQ-9 declined by 2.41 points over a median follow-up of 8 weeks (d = -0.58; 27.1% reliable improvement). Safety-relevant content appeared in 11.0% of sessions, with no confirmed safety gaps after clinician adjudication (0/50).

title: AI vs. Humans: Does AI Face Harsher Moral Judgments? A Meta-Analysis
description:
Research on how people judge AI compared to humans remains fragmented despite its criticality
in resolving a multitude of current AI ethical debates. This pre-registered meta-analysis (OSF:
10.17605/OSF.IO/GUHPQ; PROSPERO: CRD420251237117) addresses this by systematically reviewing
experimental evidence from 50 experimental studies (363 comparisons) comparing moral judgments of
human and AI agents’ decisions in moral dilemmas (e.g. the trolley problem) which were extracted from
PubMed, Web of Science and Elicit. Standardized effect sizes (Hedge’s g) were computed for two-cell
designs (Agent: Human vs. AI). Risk of bias was assessed using a pre-registered checklist for experimental
designs. Results from a three-level random-effects meta-analysis show that AI agents’ moral decisions are
judged as less morally permissible than equivalent human decisions (g = -0.08, p = 0.035). Among several
moderation analyses, perceived mental capacity (PMC) – ascribed through proxies such as agency and
experience – significantly reduced and reversed the negative effect (g = 0.11, p = 0.007). Higher PMC
corresponded to smaller or reversed differences between moral evaluations of human and AI decisions.
Interpretability was constrained by substantial heterogeneity across designs. Together, these findings
reveal asymmetries in the moral frameworks guiding evaluations of human and AI agents and point to
psychological factors that may contribute to variability in human-AI moral expectations. No external
funding.

title: Testing observation-scale linking functions between surprisal and online measures of sentence processing
description: Contextual surprisal reliably predicts online language-processing measures, but the functional form of that relationship is difficult to interpret because observed measures are not latent cognitive costs. Eye movements and event-related potentials are outputs of measurement systems, task constraints, and response definitions; therefore, nonlinear effects of surprisal on those measures can arise either before or after the latent cost that a theory may posit. This article estimates observation-scale linking functions from surprisal to online sentence-processing measures in two existing datasets: a Dutch co-registered eye-tracking/EEG corpus and an English sentence-aligned dataset with eye-movement, self-paced reading, and ERP measures. The analysis uses power-law transformations of surprisal, selected by blocked cross-validation inside the full covariate model. Dutch analyses use matched content-word observations for eye-tracking and N400 comparisons, include SUBTLEX-NL frequency, and analyze reading times in untransformed milliseconds with Gamma models, with raw-OLS and log-OLS sensitivity analyses. English source comparisons use a common observation mask for transformer and n-gram surprisal estimates. Surprisal significantly predicted every primary Dutch measure and most English measures. However, after matched exclusions, frequency control, raw-time modeling, and one-standard-error/practical-equivalence checks, the Dutch data did not require a nonlinear exponent: ordinary surprisal was practically competitive for all primary measures. The English data showed more limited and model-dependent departures, with Gamma reading-time models favoring non-unit exponents for some eye-movement measures, while N400 and P600 analyses did not provide decisive evidence for distinct nonlinear exponents. These results support surprisal as a robust predictor while showing that observation-scale linking claims require scale-sensitive diagnostics rather than inference from point estima

title: Criminal Evidence Indexes for Taxometric Investigations of Guilty-Suspect Base Rates and Classifications
description: Taxometric methods may help researchers estimate guilty-suspect base rates in the criminal justice system and develop procedures for classifying individual suspects. This program requires that criminal evidence be quantified for statistical analysis, but no appropriate indicator variables exist. We discuss the criteria for suitable taxometric indicators and outline characteristics that indexes of criminal evidence should meet. We derive quantitative indexes of four types of criminal evidence: eyewitness identifications, interrogations and confessions, forensic match evidence, and propensity evidence. We sketch how the proposed indexes could be validated within the taxometric program. Further, we illustrate how researchers can empirically probe critical assumptions underlying these indexes, quantify the sizes of departures from these idealizations, and leverage these estimates to modify and improve index calculations. The proposed indexes address an outstanding impediment to the realization of the taxometric program to study guilty-suspect base rates in the criminal justice system.

title: Scoring-Condition Drift in Rater-Scored Performance Assessment: A Feature-Warrant Framework
description: Rater-scored performance assessments support placement, certification, progress monitoring, and program evaluation only when scores retain the same meaning across administrations. This article develops a feature-warrant framework for studying scoring-condition drift: changes in the relation between observable performance features and assigned scores when prompts, rubrics, rater training, scoring interfaces, stakes, or decision rules change. The framework distinguishes uniform score shifts from changes in feature weighting, and separates rater-side drift from performer adaptation. A concrete performance-assessment ecology is used to define scoring conditions, features, and warrants before formal models are introduced. Drift is then represented through feature-by-condition interactions, transformed alignment indices, multivariate drift summaries, and decision-impact quantities. Published speaking-assessment evidence illustrates the framework: identical speech samples can support different feature weights under different rating prompts, and fluency evidence is often profile-based rather than reducible to single features. The article closes with designs for planned studies, bridge audits, small-program monitoring, and reporting decisions tied to operational consequences and score use in routine and revised assessment systems.

title: Framing effects in explanation: How win-loss framing shapes political explanations
description: People use explanation to make sense of complex real-world events, yet little work has examined whether explanations are susceptible to framing effects. In two studies, we explored whether framing the outcome of the 2024 U.S. presidential election as a win (“Why did Donald Trump win the election?”) or a loss (“Why did Kamala Harris lose the election?”) alters how people generate and evaluate explanations. In Experiment 1 (N = 301), participants listed reasons for the election outcome. Framing influenced both the number and kind of reasons used to explain the outcome. In Experiment 2 (N = 302), participants evaluated explanations while the frame was manipulated. Endorsement of explanations again depended on framing. We discuss these results in the context of two hypotheses: a memory retrieval hypothesis, in which a candidate’s name serves as a retrieval cue for generating explanations, and a pragmatic hypothesis, in which people assess the relevance of the explanans to the explanandum. While both factors may lead to a framing effect, our results indicate a strong influence of pragmatics, especially in Experiment 2 where retrieval demands are minimal. Collectively, the results demonstrate a strong framing effect on explanation. Notably, these findings run counter to prevailing theories of explanation that propose explanations are judged by their probability since probability is not affected by framing.

title: Partnership-Centered Audiology Service Model for Older Adults with Hearing Loss
description:
Purpose
	Hearing loss can affect both the individual with hearing loss and their communication partner. Perspectives on communication abilities can differ between an individual with hearing loss and their communication partner, leading to differences in perceived communication outcomes. The purpose of this mixed-methods study is to develop effective ways to involve communication partners in aural rehabilitation and measure the degree to which mismatches change following a brief virtual intervention session.
Method
	Adult clients with hearing loss and their identified communication partners completed the Social Participation Restrictions Questionnaire, Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly, and Significant Other Scale of Hearing Disability questionnaires before and shortly after the virtual intervention session. During the session, participant pairs completed a listening activity, watched a brief video about hearing loss, and answered structured interview questions.
Results
Strong, positive correlations were measured for the percentage of the conversation that the client understood, but correlations were weaker for listening effort expended by the client and their willingness to continue in conversation. Measures of agreement using all three questionnaires did not significantly improve following intervention. Main themes emerging from the interviews suggested that communication strategies organically develop within successful relationships, audiology appointments can miss the mark, and understanding the emotional impacts of hearing loss is key. 
Conclusions
	Even a brief amount of aural rehabilitation may lead clients and their communication partners to greater understanding about the experience of hearing loss and strategies for improved communication success.

title: A single perceptual comparison is sufficient, but not necessary, to induce lasting memory distortion
description: Humans constantly compare their visual memories with similar visual inputs to modify their behavior adaptively. However, basic and applied studies suggest that these comparisons can produce systematic distortions in observers’ memory reports that persist across time and contaminate subsequent reports. This has led to the hypothesis that perceptual comparisons, while adaptive, are both necessary and sufficient to produce persistent memory distortions. In three experiments, we tested this hypothesis by independently manipulating demands for perceptual comparisons and memory reports across a pair of memory tests separated by a 24-hour delay. At each test, observers were cued to recall colored object silhouettes that they had learned previously. At the first test, following cued recall, the silhouette was presented again in a similar color to serve as a perceptual probe to be compared with memory or to be used in a control task where comparisons were omitted and attention to the probe varied. Afterwards, observers either reported their memory of the recalled silhouette or not. Memory reports at the first test exhibited attractive biases toward the probe after comparisons and each of the control tasks. While biases persisted into the second test following comparisons, as previously demonstrated, they also persisted when the control task required processing of the probe that was commensurate with comparisons. In both cases, persistence was not contingent upon making an initial memory report. Therefore, a single perceptual comparison is indeed sufficient for memory distortions to persist, but persistence may be primarily determined by attentional engagement with similar visual inputs.

title: The structure and degree of social connection is associated with the structure and idiosyncrasy of social inference
description: Social connection is associated with broad aspects of social cognition. Here, we probe the nature of this association in two studies (Ns=305, 759) with college-aged samples in which we measured different aspects of social (dis)connection and performance on a measure of social inference. We find that intersubject differences in social connection mirrored intersubject differences in social inference, suggesting a shared fingerprint between the experience of one’s relationships and the perception of social information. Further, greater levels of social disconnection were associated with greater idiosyncrasy in social inference, which was largely driven by task inaccuracy. This finding suggests that social disconnection may distort internal models of mental states in a way that pulls individuals from a canonical understanding of minds. Although findings were specific to Study 2, these results provide important context to how social connection relates to social cognition and highlights social cognition as a potential intervention target.

title: Identifying the relationship between Type 1 Diabetes management and symptomology of ARFID
description: The present study aimed to identify a link between Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1D) and Avoidant-Resistant Food Intake Disorder (ARFID). Whilst previous research has identified a difference in food intake and body dissatisfaction in those with T1D, and a small amount of research identified food avoidance behaviours in those with T1D, these three factors have not been investigated together. The present study investigated food avoidance, body dissatisfaction and food frequency in those with T1D (n = 119) and without T1D (n = 119) using the Fear of Food Questionnaire (FoFQ), Body Appreciation Scale 2 (BAS-2), and the Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ). Three independent t-tests were conducted, which found those with T1D reported significantly higher food avoidance, significantly greater body dissatisfaction, yet no difference in food frequency, partially supporting the hypothesis of an alignment between T1D and ARFID due to the high food avoidance reported in those with T1D. However, this result is complicated due to no difference in food frequency between the two groups, suggesting the reported avoidance may be specific to certain foods. The small difference in body dissatisfaction could be explained by the increased prevalence of body dissatisfaction cited in those with T1D, and could reinforce this avoidance being due to reasons relating to ARFID rather than another disorder. Further research could investigate fear-based avoidance, with fear of hypoglycaemia (FoHo) and fear of hyperglycaemia (FoHe) resulting in this avoidance, strengthening a link between T1D management and ARFID.

title: Personality Traits as Moderators of Human Trust and Reliance on Large Language Model-Powered Conversational Agents: A Scoping Review and the Personality–Trust Calibration Framework
description:
Large language model (LLM)-powered conversational agents now mediate consequential decisions, yet individuals differ markedly in how far they trust and rely on them. We ask whether stable individual differences—particularly Big Five personality traits—moderate trust calibration and over-reliance in human–LLM interaction.

We conducted a scoping review following PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidance, charting 60 empirical studies (22 examining contemporary generative LLMs) identified through structured multi-source searches (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, and arXiv) and backward citation chasing. We synthesised the evidence using a structured synthesis-without-meta-analysis (SWiM) approach with vote-counting by direction of effect.

Because much of the evidence base concerns adjacent technologies, we coded every study by AI-system type and separated findings that are LLM-specific from those extrapolated from broader human–automation research.

Three patterns are robust. First, Neuroticism and trait anxiety are the most consistent individual-difference correlates of LLM over-reliance and dependency, operating through an affect-regulation and cognitive-offloading pathway. Second, Agreeableness is associated with more positive AI attitudes and greater susceptibility to AI-generated persuasion, especially under anthropomorphic design, though not straightforwardly with problematic dependence. Third, Openness predicts AI adoption, positive attitudes, and trust, but we found no direct evidence that it elevates over-reliance.

Conscientiousness shows context-dependent and sometimes opposing effects, while Extraversion exhibits only modest effects on initial trust. Across studies, dispositional propensity-to-trust and system features—chiefly the form of explanation and uncertainty communication—are more proximal predictors of reliance than broad personality traits. title: Neural and Behavioural Signatures of Statistical Learning in Aging: Evidence from Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation
description: Statistical learning (SL) enables the extraction of regularities from structured input and is thought to support visual word processing. Us- ing a Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation (FPVS) paradigm, we investi- gated whether sensitivity to frequency-based regularities is preserved in healthy aging and how such sensitivity is expressed at the neural and behavioural level. Fifty-one older adults and a comparison group of young adults completed EEG and behavioural tasks, alongside a classic visual statistical learning (VSL) task. Results revealed robust neural discrimination of frequency-based categories in older adults, indicating preserved sensitivity to statistical regularities, although responses were reduced in amplitude compared to young adults. Behaviourally, evidence of learning was weaker and more variable across tasks, and no reliable relationship emerged between neural and behavioural indices. In contrast, performance in the VSL task declined with age and was positively associated with behavioural discrimination performance. Together, these findings suggest a dissociation be- tween preserved neural sensitivity to regularities and their behavioural expression in healthy aging.

title: Examining Relationships Between Caregiver Concerns and Family and Child Characteristics in Kindergarten Children at Risk for Language and Literacy Disorders
description:
Purpose: Identification of children with language impairments often relies on caregivers raising concerns. However, caregivers may find it difficult to identify language impairment. This study examined how child and family characteristics were related to the likelihood that caregivers reported concerns about oral language and literacy to understand the possible underlying factors influencing identification. 
Method: In a larger longitudinal study, kindergarten children (N = 385) completed a battery of oral language and literacy assessments. The caregivers completed a questionnaire including demographic information (e.g., caregiver education level) and reported concerns in the areas of oral language, literacy, speech, and attention/memory. We used two multiple logistic regressions to evaluate the predictors of caregivers’ concern about (a) oral language and (b) literacy. 
Results: Among the children with language difficulties, less than 40% of caregivers reported oral language concerns. Among the children with word reading difficulty, just over half of the caregivers reported literacy concerns. Oral language scores and attention concerns were significant predictors of caregivers’ oral language concerns. Word reading scores, caregiver education, speech concerns, and attention concerns were significant predictors of literacy concern. 
Conclusions: Although interpretations of caregivers’ concerns may vary according to our provided checklist, these concerns appear to be meaningful indicators of child language and literacy difficulties. These difficulties—particularly in oral language—often go unrecognized. Our findings underscore the need for universal language screening in early education and expanded caregiver education regarding language impairment. Relying solely on caregiver concern may lead to missing children in need of services.

title: First the Rules, Then the Summary: Piloting a Design for Accurate LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
description: In clinical settings, mental health providers often have access to electronic health record (EHR) and other patient data of real clinical or predictive value. However, they rarely have the time or resources to pull it together and use it well. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) suggest they could fill this gap, but in mental-health applications LLMs often produce statements that do not match the source data. We developed a two-part synthesis pipeline. A rules-based Python component reads each patient’s scores from twelve validated questionnaires, labels them by published severity levels, and computes how they change over time. A language model then writes a prose narrative summary of the patient’s data. Our data came from a large longitudinal study of recovery after a suicidal episode, in which participants completed a battery of psychological assessments every two months. We tested the design across both open-weights and proprietary models, then evaluated it on a 25-subject cohort. For each subject we compared the constrained pipeline’s output to the same model given the same data and prompted to summarize it with no rules. Evaluation included an automated check of every numerical and categorical statement by the “harness”, which generated 2,067 checks across the three models, an independent review of the narrative prose by two raters working separately, and a clinician review (four completed out of a target of seven) whose preliminary ratings ran above the acceptability anchor on all five dimensions. Across the three models (Gemma 4 31B, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-4.1), the harness identified one substantive content error, meaning one that would change a clinician’s reading, for a rate of 0.05%, against an unconstrained baseline in which about two in five checkable numerical statements were wrong.
