title: Iconic Gestures Support L2 Word Learning through Both Semantic Disambiguation and Sensorimotor Grounding
description: Iconic gestures often facilitate second language (L2) vocabulary learning, but the mechanism underlying this benefit remains unclear. One possibility is that gestures improve learning by reducing semantic underspecification at encoding. Another is sensorimotor grounding, where gestures help bind a newly learned L2 form to perceptual and action-related aspects of the referent, producing a richer and more retrievable lexical-semantic memory trace than verbal cues alone. We examined these possibilities across four studies of novice learners acquiring Mandarin action verbs. In Study 1, gesture-supported learning yielded higher delayed translation accuracy than translation-only learning and produced some evidence of stronger semantic interference in a speeded task. In Study 2, this advantage disappeared when the non-gesture condition was enriched with example phrases that clarified the intended meaning of the verbs, supporting a semantic disambiguation account. In Study 3, a gesture advantage re-emerged when the two conditions were matched for both cue count and disambiguating information, with higher delayed translation accuracy in gesture-with-translation compared to translation-with-example. In Study 4, this advantage extended to a speeded explicit semantic relatedness judgement task, where gesture-supported learning yielded higher accuracy, greater sensitivity, and faster responses. Across studies, the findings suggest that iconic gestures support early L2 action-verb learning through two mechanisms. First, gestures reduce semantic underspecification at encoding. Second, they provide sensorimotor grounding, in that they help bind a new L2 form to action-related aspects of the referent, thereby producing a richer and more retrievable lexical-semantic memory trace than verbal cues alone.

title: Does Teacher Support Relate to Student’s Self-Efficacy for Self-Regulation? Role of ADHD Symptoms
description: Students’ capabilities for self-regulation as well as their self-efficacy for self-regulation (SESR) are important predictors of academic success and wellbeing in school. This study examines the relationship between perceived teacher support (emotional, instructional, and classroom organization) and students’ SESR among primary school children from Grades 3 and 4 (N = 1479). We also explore whether students’ self-evaluated symptoms of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) interact with the association between perceived teacher support and SESR. The more students perceived their teacher providing emotional, instructional, or classroom organization (feedback) support, the higher the students’ SESR. Second, the more students reported ADHD symptoms, the stronger the positive relationship between teacher emotional and classroom organization (structure and feedback) support and students’ SESR. The findings highlight the importance of perceived teacher support for SESR, especially for students experiencing ADHD symptoms. This finding underscores the importance of teacher support in the classroom in today’s inclusive school practices.

title: Collective Memory Modeling: Utilizing Individualized Representations to Drive Processing Models
description: This article advances a new framework for computational memory modeling that integrates individual variability in semantic representation with computational models of memory processes. Although existing approaches to computational memory modeling have provided detailed accounts of encoding, retrieval, and decision dynamics, they typically assume fixed representations, overlooking individual differences in linguistic experience. Focusing on false memory in the Deese–Roediger–McDermott (DRM; Roediger & McDermott, 1995) paradigm, individualized distributional semantic models were constructed from social media sources and embedded within the Minerva 2 model of recognition memory while holding process parameters constant. This design isolates the contribution of representational variability to memory performance. Across simulations of 2,000 individual models, substantial variability emerged in item-level predictions. When using an optimized subset of individuals models, aggregated predictions produced strong correspondence with item-level data and exhibited a robust wisdom of the crowd effect (Steyvers & Miller, 2015), where the aggregated item-level data exceeded the performance of the best performing individual model. Additional analyses demonstrated that aggregation stabilizes behavioral predictions while preserving meaningful variability arising from differences in semantic structure. These findings provide an existence proof that representational diversity alone can account for systematic variation in memory behavior and improve predictive accuracy of a proposed model. More broadly, the results highlight the importance of incorporating individualized semantic knowledge into computational models, offering a unified and ecologically valid framework that bridges representation and process in the study of human memory.

title: Similar exercise adherence and physical fitness outcomes are observed across distinct motivation profiles in older adults participating in a home-based structured exercise programme
description:
Purpose:

Motivation and self-efficacy are established predictors of engagement and persistence within structured exercise programmes; however, it remains unclear whether these psychological factors predict objective adherence metrics and associated physical fitness outcomes within home-based exercise programmes for older adults. This study adopted a person-centred approach to examine whether distinct psychological profiles predict adherence and fitness outcomes following a structured home-based exercise programme.

Methods:

Eighty-eight older adults (age = 67.2 ± 5.5 years) completed a 26-week home-based exercise programme. Objective adherence was defined as compliance with prescribed exercise volume and quantified using cumulative metabolic equivalent minutes (MET-mins) derived from heart rate–based measures of exercise intensity and duration. Psychological profiles were identified using latent profile analysis based on autonomous motivation, controlled motivation, and exercise self-efficacy. Cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, flexibility, and mobility were assessed pre- and post-intervention.

Results:

Two psychological profiles were identified: an autonomous and highly confident profile and a moderately autonomous and confident profile. Controlled motivation was comparable between profiles, and no differences were observed in baseline demographic or physiological characteristics. Adherence was high and similar across profiles (e.g., cumulative MET-mins: 129 ± 66% vs. 116 ± 38%). Both profiles demonstrated significant and comparable improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness (V̇O₂peak), muscular strength, flexibility, and mobility.

Conclusions:

Baseline differences in self-efficacy and autonomous motivation did not predict objective adherence or fitness outcomes within a structured, well-supported home-based exercise programme for older adults. title: Designing Minds: Toward Systematic Integration of Psychological Science in Design for Augmented Humanity
description:
Design for augmented humanity increasingly operates at the level of human cognition, emotion, and behaviour. As technologies extend and reconfigure human capabilities, design decisions play a constitutive role in shaping how individuals perceive, think, and act. Despite this, the integration of psychological science into design practice remains fragmented and unsystematic. While psychological concepts are widely referenced, they are often applied in selective and decontextualised ways, limiting both explanatory depth and practical effectiveness.
This paper advances the position that the central challenge is not the absence of psychological science in design, but the lack of its systematic integration. Building on this critique, it introduces a framework of levels of psychological grounding, describing progressive forms of integration from informal awareness and ad hoc application to structured incorporation in design processes, evaluation, and interdisciplinary collaboration. The framework provides a conceptual basis for analysing current practice and guiding more coherent integration.
The paper argues that such integration is essential for designing in the context of augmented humanity, where interventions increasingly influence cognition and behaviour at scale. Systematic psychological integration is therefore positioned as a necessary condition for developing design practices that are not only effective, but also transparent, accountable, and aligned with human well-being.

title: A Tutorial for Navigating Ethical Dilemmas in Research: The Case of Early Language Interventions
description: This tutorial paper aims to provide readers with tools to reflect on ethical dilemmas that illustrate how complex decisions can become when scientific goals meet real-world consequences. Through the fictional story of the Unicorn Research Team, we focus on a group of scientists, who find themselves in disagreement with each other regarding whether (or how) to be involved in an early childhood intervention aiming to change caregivers' behaviors. We introduce reflective strategies to help researchers make sense of their own intuitions and understand those of others. First, we show that individuals' views often reflect moral frameworks that incorporate consideration of duty, values and outcomes. Second, we invite readers to consider that moral intuitions emerge from human cognition. Third, we introduce Theory of Change, a method that forces us to clarify what our potential actions realistically can be, what the most important outcomes are, and what is the strength of evidence on the underlying causal chain. Rather than offering answers, this paper encourages researchers to pause, reexamine their instincts, and remain open to others' perspectives, using tools to help oneself, and each other, understand the basis for one's position.

title: Time for Consensus: Open Challenges and Recommendations for Research on Individual Differences in Statistical Learning
description: Statistical learning (SL), the ability to extract regularities from sensory input, is hypothesized to play a major role in many aspects of higher-level cognition. While earlier investigations centered on group-level effects, a growing body of research now focuses on individual differences in this ability. This consensus paper presents the collective insights of 27 researchers worldwide who are active in the field of individual differences in SL, with the goal of reflecting on the field’s progress so far while outlining key challenges going forward. Our discussion covers possible theoretical and operational definitions of SL, the trade-offs between controlled laboratory tasks and ecologically valid paradigms, considerations in interpreting correlations between SL performance and other cognitive abilities, issues of measurement reliability and statistical power, and rationales for adopting individual-differences versus group-level approaches. Based on these discussions, we outline nine actionable recommendations for the field to move forward, which are meant to lead to a new body of evidence that is more theoretically informed and more methodologically robust.

title: Revealing the Mystery of Emotions in Sounds The Theory of Musical Equilibration Explains the Impact of Ordered Sounds as the Listener’s Identification with Processes of Will
description: Science has long been concerned with the question of how it is possible for music to elicit emotions‒so far, however, with only moderate success. The theory of musical equilibration shines a light on this problem from a new perspective. The theory was first proposed in 1997 by German music theorist, Bernd Willimek, who further developed it with his wife and fellow theorist, Daniela Willimek. Music itself, the theory goes, cannot generate emotions directly. Rather, emotions should be understood as a response to the processes of will that are encoded in music. By identifying with these processes of will, listeners experience music emotionally. This is comparable to the situation of moviegoers who identify with the protagonist on screen and thereby vicariously experience emotions. In this work, the affirmative character of the major triad and the negative character of the minor triad are substantiated. According to the theory of musical equilibration, the volume at which a minor chord is played determines whether it is perceived as sorrow or anger. Furthermore, the authors discuss issues such as why a diminished seventh chord is well suited as the score for film scenes involving fear, or how an augmented chord can convey amazement and astonishment. To show the practical application of the theory of musical equilibration, the authors carried out tests with school (K-12) and university students (basic test part A, basic test part B, Rocky test).

title: From Human to AI: How Delegation to AI Shifts Moral Responsibility Attribution
description:
As AI systems increasingly make moral decisions on behalf of humans, questions arise
about how this delegation reshapes moral responsibility. Yet little is known about
whether people hold AI systems responsible for delegated moral decisions, and whether
this differs from delegating to human agents. This study examines people’s willingness
to delegate moral decisions to AI systems or human agents, and how delegation relates
to the attribution of moral responsibility. Across two studies and six moral dilemmas (N =
669), the effects of agent type (human vs. AI), domain (business vs. healthcare), and
trade-off severity (low vs. high) on delegation and responsibility attribution were
examined. Results show no evidence that delegation differed between AI systems and
humans. When decision stakes are high, delegation increases. Furthermore, delegation
is associated with a partial transfer of perceived moral responsibility toward the
delegate, to both AI systems and humans, resulting in a mostly shared responsibility
pattern between delegator and delegate. The findings challenge machine aversion
assumptions and reveal a psychological disposition to attribute responsibility to AI
systems.

title: Dimensions of Victimhood
description: Moral and political conflicts revolve around victimhood —who is harmed, how severely, and even whether harm has occurred at all. Although humans have always cared about concrete interpersonal victimhood, the complexity of modern society creates many varieties of victimhood, which we organize along two dimensions: Scale (the number of victims) and Tangibility (the concreteness of victimization). These dimensions exist in both the mind and the world and are grounded in domain-general cognitive processes: epistemic trust and numerical cognition (scale), and ontological assumptions and linguistic scaffolding (tangibility). These dimensions help explain elements of political dynamics from polarization to misinformation, help map moral cognition to cognitive science, and suggest multiple directions for future research.

title: Audiovisual Entertainment Media Narratives and Openness toward Underrepresented Groups: A Systematic Review
description: Research examining the relationship between exposure to audiovisual entertainment media narratives and openness toward underrepresented groups has been conducted across multiple disciplines, resulting in high heterogeneity in methods and fragmented findings. This systematic review synthesizes empirical studies (N = 104) across disciplines to examine this relationship and its underlying mechanisms. A comprehensive search yielded studies examining affective, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions of openness. Our synthesis revealed largely inconclusive findings across these dimensions. However, we found most evidence for associations with or effects on reduced prejudice and aversion outcomes. Additionally, we found the most conclusive evidence for outgroup identification as an underlying mechanism. The underrepresented groups for whom we found most evidence of relationships and effects were people with disabilities, disorders, and mental illness. While audiovisual entertainment media narratives can positively influence openness toward underrepresented groups, the mechanisms and conditions under which these effects occur require further investigation. Recommendations for research practices are discussed to advance understanding of entertainment media narratives in promoting openness toward underrepresented groups.

title: The FRIEND Procedure: A Fast-Friends Paradigm With Nonviolent Communication Priming for Dyadic Belonging Research
description: The Fast Friends Procedure (FFP) is a widely used paradigm for generating interpersonal closeness in stranger dyads, but standard versions specify the disclosure prompts far more clearly than they specify how participants are prepared for reciprocal vulnerability (Aron et al., 1997; Sprecher, 2021). This design note documents the FRIEND procedure: a feasibility-stage adaptation of the FFP that introduced a brief Nonviolent Communication (NVC) primer immediately before the dyadic task, paired with the development of a provisional companion measure, the Dyadic Engagement and Safety Index (DESI-14) (Rosenberg, 2003). The study ran at the University of East London with 30 participants forming 15 stranger dyads, randomised to either a 15-minute NVC primer or a duration-matched body-scan mindfulness control delivered immediately before the FFP. This note documents the FRIEND protocol in enough detail for methodological reuse. It also traces how DESI-14 emerged from an earlier DESI-12 pilot rather than presenting the instrument as a finished product without lineage. The procedure was deliverable within a single laboratory session and generated a medium between-group Inclusion of Other in the Self (IOS) signal favouring the NVC condition (U = 160.5, p = .041, rank-biserial r = .43), though a complete-case analysis reduced this to p = .058, rendering it statistically fragile and the feasibility sample was not designed for confirmatory efficacy inference (Aron et al., 1992). Pilot evidence from DESI-12 suggested ceiling-prone items and under-specified coverage of inclusion, reciprocal attunement, and non-verbal safety signalling. Three items were removed and five new items added, yielding DESI-14 as a trial-stage instrument under active development rather than a completed psychometric product. The article contributes a replicable dyadic protocol and a transparent developmental record for a still-emerging emotional-safety measure.

title: Linking behavioral and neural measures of visual search
description: Visual search is a ubiquitous behavior, yet its neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we combine behavioral modeling and fMRI to identify neural signatures of core visual search computations. Participants performed visual search tasks in which targets differed from distractors along color, shape, or both dimensions, while attentional focus was experimentally manipulated. We show that behavioral search slopes – quantifying how response time scales with set size – are mirrored by corresponding fMRI-derived slopes, such that neural responses increase systematically with set size and scale with target-distractor similarity. This correspondence identifies a neural index of search difficulty and implicates regions in mid- and higher-level visual cortex in target-template matching processes. In addition, we replicate behavioral evidence for flexible attentional weighting of feature dimensions and demonstrate that this prioritization is reflected in modulation of neural activity in a subset of higher-level visual regions. Finally, we show that fMRI responses in bidimensional search can be predicted from activity measured during unidimensional search, demonstrating that computational models of behavior generalize to neural data. Together, these findings establish a quantitative link between behavioral and neural measures of visual search and provide a framework for studying attentional guidance and feature integration in the human brain.

title: The Psychological, Emotional, and Relational Impact of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury on Parents: A Meta-Analysis Protocol
description: Objective: This meta-analysis aims to systematically synthesise the evidence on the psychological, emotional, and relational experiences of parents of individuals who engage in non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI). Introduction: NSSI is a significant public health concern associated with adverse outcomes for both individuals and their families. While a substantial body of research has examined NSSI among young people, less attention has been given to its impact on parents and caregivers. Existing studies reveal that parents often experience considerable psychological distress, emotional burden, and disruption to family functioning following awareness of their child’s NSSI. However, a quantitative synthesis is needed to clarify the magnitude and direction of these parental outcomes and to identify gaps in the current evidence base to inform future research and the development of targeted supports for parents. Inclusion criteria: The review will include empirical studies examining parents or caregivers of individuals who engage in NSSI. Eligible studies must report at least one outcome related to parental psychological, emotional, or relational experiences. Methods: The review will follow the PRISMA guideline for meta-analyses. Electronic searches will be conducted across Medline, Scopus, ProQuest, and Web of Science. Two reviewers will independently screen studies, extract data, and assess risk of bias using standardised tools. Pooled effect sizes and random effect models will be calculated using meta-analysis. Results and Conclusion: This meta-analysis will provide a synthesis of the psychological, emotional, and relational experiences of parents of individuals who engage in NSSI and identify gaps in the literature. Findings will inform future research and support the development of evidence-informed interventions and supports for parents and caregivers of individuals who self-injure.

title: Age and Gender Differences in Body Talk Frequency and Longitudinal Associations Between Body Talk and Body Image Variables
description: The first purpose of this study was to investigate age and gender differences in three types of body talk: negative fat talk, negative muscle talk, and positive body talk. The second purpose was to examine longitudinal associations between body talk and body image variables at the within-person level, while distinguishing them from between-person associations. In this three-wave online study, a total of 5,707 women and men aged 15–94 years participated in the Wave 1 survey, and 3,597 completed two follow-up surveys administered at two-month intervals. Participants completed measures of body talk, body fat dissatisfaction, drive for muscularity, body appreciation, and the internalization of thin and athletic body ideals at each wave. Analyses of Wave 1 data indicated that negative fat talk was characteristic of women in their teens and twenties, whereas negative muscle talk was characteristic of men in the same age groups. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel model analyses of the three-wave data revealed that most longitudinal associations between body talk and body image variables at the within-person level were not statistically significant across age and gender groups. In contrast, significant between-person associations were observed across age groups in both women and men, including positive correlations between negative fat talk and body fat dissatisfaction and between positive body talk and body appreciation. These longitudinal findings suggest that previously reported associations between body talk and body image variables may largely reflect relatively stable individual differences, with less clear evidence for a mutually reinforcing relationship between body talk and body image variables.

title: Learning in context: Socioemotional stimuli enhance cognitive learning processes but not psychophysiological engagement in early adolescence
description: Throughout development, we learn through trial and error in the face of uncertainty. This ‘reinforcement learning’ supports youth’s ability to adapt to environmental demands. Theory suggests that early experiences optimize learning to prioritize socially relevant cues across multiple levels of analysis. Yet, experimental paradigms often use abstract stimuli and limit measures of learning to behavioral summaries such as task accuracy. This study uses computational models grounded in reinforcement learning and dynamic systems frameworks to examine how socioemotional context modulates cognitive and psychophysiological learning processes. In a sample of 56 youth aged 12-15 years, a within-person experimental design quantified continuous behavior and heart rate (~700 observations of behavior and heart rate, per person) during an adapted reinforcement learning task with stimuli that varied in socioemotional relevance. A series of Bayesian multilevel models revealed that, compared to traditionally-used non-emotional stimuli, learning from stimuli high in socioemotional arousal enhanced behavioral performance. Specifically, computational models suggested that socioemotional salience may elicit faster value-updating processes and a qualitative shift to more exploitative decision-making. Underlying psychophysiological engagement was modulated by heightened sensitivity to learning from rewards, showing faster value-updating in the context of rewards aligned with more optimal psychophysiological flexibility and organization. Together, these findings clarify the contexts and modulatory processes that shape developmental learning mechanisms.

title: “Unbrake my rejected heart”: Cardiac slowing when maltreated youth reconnect with peers who resemble caregivers
description: Adverse caregiving experiences are thought to bias internal representations of self and others, giving rise to negative expectations that generalize to new encounters. However, few studies examine whether cues signaling resemblance to caregivers selectively increase the odds of generalization. In this preregistered study, 133 participants were assessed for maltreatment at two waves (n = 65 maltreated; ages 4–16 and 11–24 years). At the second wave, participants played Cyberball. Following social exclusion, participants re-engaged with two novel co-players, who ostensibly introduced themselves via self-descriptive blurbs: The Target implicitly resembled the participant’s caregiver, whereas the Control resembled someone else’s caregiver. The co-players threw the ball to participants (re-inclusions) or not (re-exclusions) at equal rates. We assessed event-related cardiac slowing, a correlate of expectancy violation. Cardiac slowing to Target was most pronounced in younger participants and declined with age, suggesting that caregiver cues exert a stronger influence on peer interactions at younger ages. Supporting our pre-registered hypotheses, during re-exclusions, maltreated participants showed greater cardiac slowing to Control vs. Target, whereas nonmaltreated participants exhibited the opposite pattern. We conclude that, for maltreated individuals, re-exclusion violates expectancies less when stemming from caregiver-like targets, implying that resemblance cues trigger selective generalization during early psychophysiological processing.

title: Scalable estimation of continuous perceptual representations from human judgements and computer vision: An application to melanoma identification
description: Human perceptual judgements are central to many classification and decision tasks, yet they are often measured using coarse, discrete ratings that obscure the continuous structure of underlying perceptual representations. We present a scalable measurement framework for recovering continuous, ratio-scale perceptual representations from pairwise human judgements using the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model. We apply this framework to a large natural image set (10,000 skin lesion images) to derive interpretable perceptual representations of dimensions central to melanoma risk assessment: shape asymmetry, border irregularity, and colour variance. We evaluate the face validity and reliability of these perceptual measures and compare them to deterministic computer vision estimates of the same features. The resulting representations show moderate correspondence, indicating partial overlap but substantial non-redundant information. We demonstrate the functional utility of these measurements by evaluating classification performance using models trained on human-derived perceptual measures, computer vision estimates, and their combination. We found that integrating human and computational representations yields improved diagnostic discrimination relative to either source alone, illustrating representational complementarity. The proposed pairwise comparison and modelling approach we present enables efficient, scalable recovery of continuous perceptual representations for large stimulus sets and provides a principled framework for comparing representations across human and machine systems.

title: Aloneness and Identity Across the Lifespan
description: This study considered how attitudes towards being alone develop across the lifespan and whether and how they differ between generations.  Drawing on Erikson’s theory of identity development we asked whether developing aloneness attitudes might interlink with identity development, and whether having a strong sense of integrated identity may promote positive attitudes about aloneness. We asked 95 adult participants to share qualitative stories about their experiences of being alone across the lifespan. Analysis of their stories, using framework analysis, allowed for comparison across generations. We developed three themes: 1) Identity integration in youth supports positive attitudes towards aloneness across the lifespan; 2) Unstable or lacking identity integration may be linked to acute loneliness in middle age; and 3) Active self-reflection promotes identity integration and protects against loneliness across generations. These findings suggest that identity development, particularly in early life, may be important to the promotion of a positive attitude towards aloneness and may protect against loneliness across the lifespan. The benefits of self-reflection are also highlighted.

title: Spiritual Patience: Preliminary Results
description: In these preliminary results, we develop and validate a measure of spiritual patience. Spiritual patience is defined as the virtue of abiding well (not poorly) with transcendent silence, absence, or obscurity, motivated by a longing and love for the divine or a transcendent force. In Studies 1 and 2, spiritual patience is revealed to be a one factor, 7-item scale and excellent internal consistency. In Study 3, our measure of spiritual patience demonstrated good internal consistency, discriminant validity, convergent validity, and incremental validity. In Study 4, spiritual patience was found to mediate the relations between spiritual yearning and meaning in life as well as depression. Overall, these results put forward a sound measure of spiritual patience and demonstrate this virtue's importance in spiritual flourishing.

title: Nothing “Evaluative“ about Evaluative Priming?  Semantic Relatedness Beyond Evaluation Is Not Necessary for a Facilitation of Evaluative Judgements
description: Ever since Zajonc proposed that preferences need no inferences, psychologists have debated whether evaluations can be conceptualized and measured independently of co-activated semantic content. One prominent arena for this debate has been the Evaluative Priming Task, which tracks the effects of conflicting or congruent evaluative relationships between stimuli. Surprisingly, two prior lines of research found that effects of evaluative congruency in the task do not emerge in the absence of additional semantic relationships. This not only conflicts with other findings, but also challenges dominant theoretical accounts of the task, whose assumptions entail that congruency effects should arise irrespectively. In Studies 1 and 2 (Ns=81, 85), we re-examine these two lines of research and show that when vulnerabilities in the original experimental and analytical designs are rectified, evaluative congruency effects do reliably occur (even in the absence of strong semantic relationships). A third study (N=80), that implements strong semantic relationships under especially controlled conditions, also yields reliable congruency effects. In Study 4 (N=81), the trials with low semantic relatedness from the first three studies are combined, replicating consistent and reliable, but small congruency effects. Our results thereby strengthen models that accommodate an independent role of evaluations, and we illustrate how these models might be modified to account for an augmenting influence of semantic relatedness. Currently, in domains for which evaluations and their measurement are integral (like the measurement of race-based evaluations, consumer or health behavior), the pronounced and potentially biasing effects of semantic relatedness remain largely unrecognized as a serious confound.

title: Dissociating behavioral, neural and experiential effects of prefrontal HD-tDCS during conflict resolution
description: Inconsistent evidence regarding the cognitive effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) highlights the need for more comprehensive approaches to assess its impact. This study aimed to investigate the effects of high-definition tDCS (HD-tDCS) on conflict resolution by combining behavioral, neural, and subjective experience measures. Sixty participants were randomly assigned to anodal, cathodal, or sham HD-tDCS groups and completed a 30-minute flanker task. EEG was recorded during the first and last blocks (without stimulation), while stimulation was applied during the intermediate blocks of the task. Using a multidimensional methodological approach including Drift-Diffusion Modeling (DDM), EEG spectral analysis, Lempel-Ziv complexity, and Temporal Experience Tracing (TET), we assessed the cognitive, neural, and phenomenological effects of stimulation. Behavioral results indicated no significant improvements in reaction times or accuracy across the stimulation groups. Similarly, DDM parameters showed no effect of HD-tDCS on latent cognitive processes. However, EEG data revealed a significant reduction in neural complexity in the anodal group during resting-state, suggesting a stabilization or reorganization of neural dynamics. Subjective experience analysis identified two distinct clusters of task-related feelings, though time spent in these experiential states did not differ between groups. Interestingly, sensation of stimulation was significantly higher for anodal stimulation than sham when analyzed as a single dimension. Despite null behavioral effects, this study provides important insights into the neural and subjective responses to HD-tDCS and highlights the value of integrating complementary multidimensional approaches to better characterize brain stimulation effects. These findings contribute to the ongoing debate about the efficacy of tDCS in cognitive enhancement.

title: Exploring the Lower-Order Structure of Trait Disinhibition
description: Disinhibition is a core domain across models of personality and psychopathology, and it is robustly associated with many important outcomes. Disagreement remains concerning its lower-order structure, as existing models and measures differ in the number, content, and breadth of its underlying facets. This preregistered study examined the hierarchical structure of Disinhibition as assessed via self-report pathological personality measures using item-level analyses. A pool of Disinhibition-related items (138 items) was assessed using Goldberg’s “bass-ackward” factor-analytic (2006) procedure in an undergraduate sample (N = 929). Results supported a hierarchical four-factor solution comprising Rashness, Unreliability, Risk Taking, and Distractibility. These factors showed strong convergence with PID-5 and CAT-PD Disinhibition, relatively distinct profiles of association with varying personality traits, and meaningful relations with externalizing and internalizing criteria. Content reflecting overcontrol (e.g., perfectionism) was included in the pool but was not featured in the derived structure. Implications for models and measurement of Disinhibition are discussed.

title: Parsing Causal Relations in Social Science Publications
description: Systematically cataloging causal claims made in the social sciences and parsing them into structured cause-effect relations is vital for accumulating knowledge and testing theories across large bodies of literature. Manual review is infeasible due to the scale of the literature and linguistic ambiguity, while existing automated methods often lack domain specificity or fail to extract specific cause-effect pairs. We introduce a BERT-based multitask deep learning model trained on a novel, domain-specific benchmark dataset of 3,014 annotated sentences from social science papers. The model simultaneously (1) identifies sentences containing causal claims, (2) parses them by extracting cause and effect spans (including mediating variables via a new annotation schema), and (3) links the associated causal pairs. The model achieved a reliability level matching that of human coders (Krippendorff’s α = 0.80) and robust F1 performance across configurations. The model and dataset are available as validated, open-source resources that offer a scalable, transparent, and reproducible alternative to manual annotation. It can be used to automatically catalogue causal claims, thereby contributing to research synthesis and theory development.

title: Bias Feedback as Moral Threat: Shame, Defensiveness, and Short-Term Self-Concept Change
description: Bias feedback indicating that one's responses may reflect racial bias despite egalitarian intentions can function as a moral threat to the self. Across three studies and four samples (N = 1,266), we tested whether high (vs. low) bias feedback elicits shame and defensiveness, whether bias awareness shapes those responses, and how shame and defensiveness relate to self-concept clarity, moral self-image, and self-esteem after feedback. High (vs. low) bias feedback increased both shame and defensiveness. Bias awareness was positively associated with shame and lower defensiveness, though effects varied across studies. Shame was most consistently associated with lower self-concept clarity, moral self-image, and self-esteem, indicating disruption in both self-understanding and self-evaluation. Defensiveness followed a narrower pattern in Studies 2 and 3, linked to relatively preserved self-concept clarity alongside lower moral self-image and self-esteem. Shame and defensiveness appear to be distinct responses to bias feedback with different short-term consequences for self-understanding and self-evaluation.

title: A systematic review of factors associated with adherence to prophylaxis during chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear emergencies
description: Post-exposure prophylaxis may be recommended during chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear (CBRN) emergencies and must often be initiated rapidly to be effective. Understanding factors that affect uptake (initiation) and subsequent adherence (completion) will help to minimise barriers and support adherence during emergencies. This systematic review synthesises evidence on factors associated with uptake of and adherence to prophylaxis following exposure to anthrax, radiation, smallpox, or viral pandemic diseases such as influenza or COVID-19. The review was pre-registered (https://osf.io/f5nmw). We searched Medline, Embase, APA PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, and subject specific databases, with no language or date restrictions. PRISMA and synthesis without meta-analysis (SWiM) guidelines were followed alongside NICE recommendations for risk of bias assessment. Data were extracted on factors associated with, and interventions targeting, uptake and adherence to prophylaxis across the four scenarios. Of 17,217 records screened, 21 studies were included. Uptake and adherence varied widely. Evidence on associated factors was inconsistent and generally of low certainty. Few scenario-specific differences were identified; variation was more strongly associated with population and contextual factors. Common barriers included concerns about side effects, low perceived risk, and lack of trust in information sources. Evidence on the effectiveness of interventions was limited to two studies, at high risk of bias. In conclusion, preparedness should prioritise addressing shared motivational and practical barriers across settings. There is a critical need to develop and evaluate interventions to support timely uptake and adherence to prophylaxis before emergencies occur.

title: Good Vibrations: A Content Analysis of Depictions of Sex Toy Use in Mainstream Heterosexual Pornography
description: Recent rapid advances and diffuse uptake of technology have increased accessibility of forms of technology designed to enhance sexual experiences. Analysis of depictions of sex toy use in pornography provides a means of estimating whether such “sextech” have been integrated into the sexual norms of the viewing population. This study aimed to investigate how sex toys are depicted in mainstream, heterosexual, online pornography. Heterosexual pornographic videos featuring sex toys (N = 100) from two highly popular sites, were content coded based on a formal coding process developed to capture video characteristics. Videos featured up to three types of toys (M = 1.19), with the most frequently depicted toys being vibrators (58%), followed by anal toys (30%), dildos (24%), and finally penile strokers (7%). Toys were most commonly used on the female actor (85%), and were depicted as inducing their orgasm in 33% of videos. Apart from sex toy use, the most commonly portrayed sexual behaviors included fellatio, vaginal intercourse, and manual penile stimulation. This study illuminates how mainstream pornography depicts the integration of sex toys into female–male sexual behaviors. Given that people often use pornography as a source of sexual information, porn depicting sex toy use may inform real-world attitudes and expectations.

title: Disentangling Within- and Between-Subject Correlations in Cognitive Models: The Essential Role of Hierarchical Estimation
description: Cognitive models, such as evidence-accumulation models, are increasingly used in individual differences research in psychology and neuroscience. By computing correlations between cognitive model parameters across participants, researchers aim to understand how the psychological processes the parameters represent relate to one another and jointly determine performance. It is generally acknowledged that cognitive models can be challenging to estimate due to strong within-subject correlations among the parameters, which are embedded in the model's likelihood function. What is less often recognized, however, is that within-subject correlations can also distort correlations computed between parameters estimated with non-hierarchical methods, so they no longer reflect true individual differences, potentially leading to misleading conclusions. Here we illustrate this pitfall of non-hierarchical estimation and show how appropriately parameterized, descriptively adequate hierarchical models can mitigate the problem by effectively separating within- and between-subject sources of variation. We then offer recommendations for identifying and guarding against the inferential biases resulting from the strong within-subject correlations inherent in many cognitive models.
